items.stem: Noah, who has diabetes, injected insulin and skipped lunch and became confused. In this state Noah hit Mei, a colleague, causing a broken nose. Discuss which defence Noah may rely on and its effect. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: insanity: defect of reason from a disease of the mind (internal cause) so that D did not know the nature and quality of the act or that it was wrong (M'Naghten; Sullivan; Hennessy); non-insane automatism: total loss of control caused by an external factor (Hill v Baxter; Quick; A-G's Ref No 2 of 1992); self-induced automatism is no defence to basic intent offences if D was reckless (R v Bailey). Application: Noah injected insulin and skipped lunch; the cause was external (insulin), so non-insane automatism (R v Quick). Conclusion: Noah is likely to rely on external (insulin), so non-insane automatism (R v Quick), leading to a complete acquittal, unless self-induced recklessly (R v Bailey).

items.answer: For: loss of control need not be sudden, helping abused victims; fear of serious violence trigger; revenge excluded; sexual infidelity excluded. items.stem: Isla threw a brick through the window of a house occupied by Grace outside a shop in Singapore. Grace, who was 90 years old and obviously frail, fell and hit their head on the pavement and died. Discuss whether Isla is guilty of unlawful act manslaughter. Explain the relevant law, apply it to the facts and evaluate the strength of any arguments available.
items.answer: Law: there must be an unlawful act that is a crime (R v Lamb; R v Franklin); the act must be dangerous: sober and reasonable people would recognise the risk of some harm (R v Church; DPP v Newbury and Jones); the reasonable person knows what D knew or would have seen (R v Dawson; R v Watson); the act must cause the death, and D need not foresee harm. Application: Isla's act was a criminal damage, a criminal act; Grace's condition was obvious to any reasonable person present (R v Watson); the jury must decide whether a sober and reasonable person would recognise a risk of some harm from the act; causation: Grace's death followed the act; the thin skull rule applies. Conclusion: Isla is likely to be guilty of unlawful act manslaughter if the act was dangerous in the Church sense; the victim's condition being obvious to any reasonable person present (R v Watson) affects this.

items.stem: Elena, who has diabetes, injected insulin and skipped lunch and became confused. In this state Elena hit Nadia, a colleague, causing a broken nose. Discuss which defence Elena may rely on and its effect. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: insanity: defect of reason from a disease of the mind (internal cause) so that D did not know the nature and quality of the act or that it was wrong (M'Naghten; Sullivan; Hennessy); non-insane automatism: total loss of control caused by an external factor (Hill v Baxter; Quick; A-G's Ref No 2 of 1992); self-induced automatism is no defence to basic intent offences if D was reckless (R v Bailey). Application: Elena injected insulin and skipped lunch; the cause was external (insulin), so non-insane automatism (R v Quick). Conclusion: Elena is likely to rely on external (insulin), so non-insane automatism (R v Quick), leading to a complete acquittal, unless self-induced recklessly (R v Bailey).
